title: DeltaNp63alpha‑mediated regulation of tumor‑associated genes and pathways in hepatocellular carcinoma progression.
authors: Lin, Xiaowen; Peng, Anghui; Zhang, Min; Yu, Xinyang
abstract: DeltaNp63alpha is key in cellular development and epithelial tumors; however, its role in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains unclear. In the present study, the oncogenic role and molecular functions of DeltaNp63alpha in HCC were investigated. Analysis of The Cancer Genome Atlas revealed an association between p63 expression and patient survival. DeltaNp63alpha overexpression in SNU387 cells notably enhanced cell proliferation and migration, supporting its role in promoting aggressive HCC phenotypes. Transcriptome analysis revealed extensive DeltaNp63alpha‑associated transcriptional changes, with differentially expressed genes enriched in tumor‑associated processes, including 'Wnt signaling pathway', 'Notch signaling pathway', 'cell adhesion molecules' and 'extracellular matrix organization'. Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing revealed widespread DeltaNp63alpha binding in promoter‑proximal and ‑distal regulatory regions, suggesting potential involvement in transcriptional regulation through both proximal and distal genomic elements. DeltaNp63alpha upregulation was also associated with increased CCCTC‑binding factor (CTCF) occupancy near the promoters of tumor‑associated genes and these gained CTCF sites were enriched for p63 motifs. Collectively, the present findings identified DeltaNp63alpha as an oncogenic regulator of HCC and suggest that it may regulate tumor‑associated gene programs through coordinated proximal and distal chromatin regulatory mechanisms.

title: Ryder: Epigenome normalization using a two-tier model and internal reference regions.
authors: Cao, Yaqiang; Ge, Guangzhe; Zhao, Keji
abstract: MOTIVATION: Sequencing-based epigenomic profiling methods are powerful but suffer from technical variability that complicates cross-sample comparisons and can obscure true biological signals. While existing normalization methods using spike-in controls or computational approaches have been proposed, they often rely on assumptions that may not hold across diverse experimental conditions or require additional data types. RESULTS: We present Ryder, a flexible and robust Python package for the normalization of epigenomic signal tracks. Ryder leverages stable internal reference regions, such as invariant CTCF binding sites, to correct for technical artifacts genome-wide. Our results show that it effectively adjusts both background noise and signal intensity, ensuring accurate signal alignment across samples while preserving genuine biological differences. We demonstrate that Ryder performs robustly across diverse assays including DNase-seq, CUT&RUN, ATAC-seq, MNase-seq, and ChIP-seq, with or without spike-in controls. By reducing technical noise, Ryder improves the detection of genuine biological changes, such as quantitative reduction of chromatin accessibility at key enhancer elements by depletion of BRG1, a key subunit of the chromatin remodeling BAF complexes. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The Ryder source code, documentation and test data are freely available at: https://github.com/YaqiangCao/ryder. The software version used in this study is archived at Zenodo: https://zenodo.org/records/21267457. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: A transcriptional cofactor GRIP1 drives PPARgamma DNA binding and p300-dependent enhancer activity during homeostatic macrophage polarization.
authors: Dacic, Marija; Stein, William J; Yuan, Ruoxi; Deochand, Dinesh K; Morrison, Joshua K; Seide, Ketsia; Chinenov, Yurii; Rogatsky, Inez
abstract: Homeostatic macrophages maintain tissue health and resolve inflammation. Upon sustained exposure to type II cytokine IL4, transcription factors STAT6, KLF4, EGR2 and a ligand-regulated nuclear receptor PPARgamma orchestrate the M2(IL4) 'polarization', marked by enhancer RNA (eRNA) production near multiple M2 genes. The mechanisms of enhancer activation by unliganded PPARgamma are poorly understood. We interrogated cofactor requirements for PPARgamma-driven gene expression in M2(IL4), including those lacking PPARgamma or a ligand-dependent nuclear receptor coregulator NCoA2/GRIP1 vs. macrophages treated with the PPARgamma agonist rosiglitazone. As expected, rosiglitazone activated conventional PPARgamma targets; GRIP1 deletion blunted their induction and depleted GRIP1-interacting histone acetyltransferase p300 from PPARgamma-bound sites. Surprisingly, GRIP1 colocalized with unliganded PPARgamma in M0 and M2(IL4), and GRIP1 ablation dramatically reduced genome-wide DNA binding of PPARgamma itself while promoting broad deposition of CTCF insulator. Functionally, GRIP1 deletion mirrored PPARgamma deficiency, establishing GRIP1 as a central regulator of unliganded PPARgamma DNA binding, required for both eRNA and mRNA transcription of PPARgamma targets in homeostatic macrophages.

title: Quantifying the impact of genetic mutations on enhancer dynamics.
authors: Das, Maitreya; Banerjee, Deepro; Hossain, Ayaan; Jensen, Matthew; Mogre, Saie; Sun, Jiawan; Mao, Joseph; Glick, Adam B; Salis, Howard M; Girirajan, Santhosh
abstract: Transcriptional regulation is mediated by enhancers, yet how genetic perturbations alter enhancer activity and gene expression remains unclear. We develop UDI-UMI-STARR-seq, integrating dual indexes and unique molecular identifiers, and combine it with RNA-seq to profile perturbation-associated changes in enhancer activity and gene expression. We apply this approach to 253,632 fragments representing 46,142 cell type-specific candidate enhancers and assess the impact of CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of six transcription factors (ATF2, CTCF, FOXA1, LEF1, TCF7L2, and SCRT1). We identify responsive fragments that are repressed or induced and enriched for p53 family motifs. Enhancer-gene mapping reveals associations between responsive fragments and gene expression changes, including Wnt/p53 targets after ATF2 or LEF1 depletion. A deep learning model recapitulates enhancer grammar, including cooperative motif syntax and flanking sequence context. Applying this framework to 16p12.1 deletion identifies responsive fragments associated with genes involved in neuronal function, providing a scalable readout of enhancer dynamics across genetic perturbations.

title: Directionality of transcriptional regulatory elements.
authors: Chen, You; Shah, Sagar R; Leung, Alden K; Paramo, Mauricio I; Gonzales, Caralyn; Cochran, Kelly; Wang, Austin; Kundaje, Anshul; Clark, Andrew G; Lis, John T; Yu, Haiyuan
abstract: Divergent transcription is a critical marker of active transcriptional regulatory elements (TREs), including enhancers and promoters, in mammals. However, distal elements with unidirectional transcriptional patterns are often overlooked, leaving their identity and function poorly understood. Here, we perform a systematic comparison between divergent and unidirectional elements, revealing their distinct architectural and functional features. Our analysis also shows that unidirectional elements have younger sequence ages and are under weaker evolutionary constraints than divergent elements, suggesting that they may represent a unique category of genomic regulatory function with more recent origins. Furthermore, we investigate factors involved in transcriptional directionality at TREs, with CTCF and ZNF143 showing dual, position-dependent roles in transcriptional modulation. Overall, the elucidation of directionality enhances our understanding of the diverse architectural models, functional features, evolutionary dynamics, and regulatory logic of TREs.

title: Guanine content in the CTCF motif encodes a vulnerability to persistent, alcohol-induced redistribution
authors: Nolan B; Puspo JA; Querry-Peterson IM; Maurina S; Wright RA; Schmitz A; Jacobsen LE; Ortiz C; Reznicek TE; Ethell A; Harris HL; Cummings CT; Rowley MJ
abstract: Alcohol consumption is a leading contributor to the global disease burden, yet its molecular consequences remain incompletely understood. Ethanols first metabolite, acetaldehyde, modifies guanine to form DNA adducts and DNA-protein crosslinks that block elongating RNA polymerase II. Because acetaldehyde acts specifically on guanine, we hypothesized that chromatin features would be disrupted in a sequence-dependent rather than stochastic manner. Here we confirm that alcohol exposure displaces elongating RNA polymerase II (RNAPIIs2p) from gene bodies, relocating to promoters. In addition to this confirmation, we found that RNAPIIs2p also relocates to discrete guanine-rich intergenic CTCF sites. Loci with high guanine content at the CTCF motifs zinc finger 5 (ZF5) binding position showed the largest increase in both CTCF and cohesin (RAD21), with CTCF occupancy changes persisting even six days after alcohol withdrawal. Surprisingly, using Hi-C, we found that these changes to CTCF and cohesin do not impact the pronounced structural CTCF loops, but are instead primarily associated with altered guanine-rich enhancer-promoter contacts that connect to lasting changes to gene expression. Beyond our cell-line model, the same sequence rule accounts for altered CTCF occupancy in a mouse starvation (metabolic stress) model and in the placentae after paternal alcohol exposure. Together these findings link alcohol exposure to sequence-directed changes to chromatin whose rules are conserved in alcohol-associated disease.

title: A role for CIZ1, a Nuclear Matrix Protein Overexpressed in Cancer Cells, in Controlling the Initiation of DNA Replication
authors: Hossain M; Tramantano M; Naik S; Stillman B
abstract: DNA replication licensing is tightly coordinated with cell-cycle progression to ensure genome stability. Here we demonstrate that CIZ1, a nuclear matrix scaffold protein in human cells, coordinates DNA replication licensing through direct interactions with the Origin Recognition Complex (ORC), CDC6, and Cyclins E/A–CDK2. The C-terminal zinc finger region of CIZ1 mediates binding to the cyclin-binding motifs of ORC1 and CDC6, and Cyclin–CDK-dependent phosphorylation regulates these interactions. Cell cycle analyses demonstrated a dynamic association of CIZ1 with ORC1 and CDC6. Functional studies showed that CIZ1 depletion impaired MCM loading, reduced DNA synthesis, delayed S-phase progression and inhibited cell proliferation. Cancer cells overexpressing CIZ1 exhibited an enhanced dependency on its expression, and CRISPR tiling screens identified the C-terminal regulatory region containing cyclin-binding motifs and CDK phosphorylation sites as essential for cell proliferation. Acute degradation of CIZ1 further revealed an unexpected role in maintaining CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) occupancy at specific genomic loci and regulating transcriptional programs associated with cell adhesion and migration, indicating that CIZ1 links DNA replication with higher-order genome organization. Finally, depletion of CIZ1 significantly suppressed colorectal tumor growth in xenograft models. Together, these findings establish CIZ1 as a multifunctional scaffold that integrates DNA replication licensing, Cyclin– CDK signaling, and chromatin architecture.
